parole.testo: From Latin -phila, from Ancient Greek φίλος (phílos, “dear, beloved”).
From Middle Dutch ame, aem, from Late Latin ama (Latin hama), from Ancient Greek ἄμη (ámē, “bucket”), ἀμάω (amáō, “to gather, harvest”), of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: archangel, member of a high one of the nine choirs (orders) of angels
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin archangelus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχάγγελος (arkhángelos). Equivalent to aarts- + engel.

parole.significato: abacus (arithmetic calculation device, usually with beads on rods)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abacus, from Ancient Greek ἄβαξ (ábax), possibly from a Semitic source; compare Hebrew אָבָק (avák, “dust”).
From Middle Dutch absinthium, from Latin absinthium, from Ancient Greek ἀψίνθιον (apsínthion). In the current spelling from French absinthe.

parole.significato: an abbot, monastic superior of an abbey
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch abbet, ultimately from Latin abbās, from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), from Aramaic אבא, from Proto-Semitic *ʾab-.

parole.significato: a shrub or tree of a species that belongs to the genus Acacia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin acacia, from Ancient Greek ἀκακία (akakía).
Borrowed from Latin acadēmicus, from Ancient Greek ἀκαδημικός (akadēmikós).

parole.significato: acolyte, lesser clergyman who only received the four lower ordinations
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch acolijt, from Late Latin acolythus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos, “follower, attendant”), from Ancient Greek κέλευθος (kéleuthos, “path”), from Proto-Indo-European *kel- with copulative ἀ- (a-).

parole.significato: agrimony, plant of the genus Agrimonia
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch agrimonie, from Latin agrimōnia, from argemōnia, from Ancient Greek ἀργεμώνη (argemṓnē).
From Middle Dutch alphabeet, from Latin alphabētum, from Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos).

parole.significato: aloe, succulent of the genus Aloe
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch aloe, from Latin aloē, from Ancient Greek ἀλόη (alóē).
From Latin amarantus, from Ancient Greek ἀμάραντος (amárantos).
Ultimately from Latin ambrosia, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀμβροσία (ambrosía).
Borrowed from Latin amphibrachys, from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβραχυς (amphíbrakhus).
Borrowed from modified Latin amnesia, from Ancient Greek ἀμνησία (amnēsía, “forgetfulness”).
From Latin amnion (“membrane around a fetus”), from Ancient Greek ἀμνίον (amníon, “bowl in which the blood of victims was caught”).
Borrowed from Latin amoeba, from Ancient Greek ἀμοιβή (amoibḗ, “change”), referring to constantly changing shape of these organisms.

parole.significato: amorphous, shapeless (lacking a definite form or clear shape)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin amorphus, from Ancient Greek ἄμορφος (ámorphos).

parole.significato: anamnesis (patient's account of their medical history)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin anamnesis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάμνησις (anámnēsis).

parole.significato: anemia, a medical condition with a decreased amount of hemoglobin, hindering oxygen transport
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin anaemia, from Ancient Greek ἀναιμία (anaimía).

parole.significato: anemone, plant or flower of the genus Anemone
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin anemōnē, from Ancient Greek ἀνεμώνη (anemṓnē).
Borrowed from Latin anaesthēsia, from Ancient Greek ἀναισθησία (anaisthēsía), from ἀν- (an-, “not”) with αἴσθησις (aísthēsis, “sensation”). Equivalent to an- + esthesie.
Borrowed from Latin antidotum, from Ancient Greek ἀντίδοτος (antídotos, “antidote, remedy”), from ἀντιδίδωμι (antidídōmi, “to give in return, repay”).
Ultimately from Late Latin antitheticus, from Ancient Greek ἀντιθετικός (antithetikós). Equivalent to antithese + -isch.
Borrowed from Latin aoristus, from Ancient Greek ἀόριστος (aóristos).
Borrowed from Latin aphelium, from Ancient Greek ἀπό (apó, “from”) + ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”) (modelled after apogaeum). Compare perihelion.
Borrowed from New Latin apnoea, from the Ancient Greek ἄπνοια (ápnoia), formed from ἀ- (a-, “absence of”) + πνοή (pnoḗ, “breathing”).
From Apocalyps (“Revelations”), from Middle Dutch apocalypsis, from Latin apocalypsis, from Ancient Greek ἀποκάλυψις (apokálupsis).
Ultimately from Latin apocalyptica, from Ancient Greek ἀποκαλυπτικα (apokaluptika). Equivalent to apocalyps + -iek.

parole.significato: apocalyptic (pertaining to the Book of Revelations or the religious genre in general)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin apocalypticus, from Ancient Greek ἀποκαλυπτικός (apokaluptikós). Equivalent to Apocalyps + -isch; some senses refer to apocalyps instead.

parole.significato: apocope (loss or omission of a sound or syllable from the end of a word)
parole.testo: First attested in 1550. Learned borrowing from Late Latin apocopē, derived from Ancient Greek ἀποκοπή (apokopḗ), ἀποκόπτω (apokóptō, “to cut off, to hew”).
Borrowed from Latin apocryphus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόκρυφος (apókruphos). Influenced by German apokryph.
From Latin apodīcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀποδεικτός (apodeiktós, “demonstrable”), from ἀποδείκνυμι (apodeíknumi, “demonstrate”).
Borrowed from Late Latin apoplexia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξία (apoplēxía).

parole.significato: apostle (disciple of Christ; missionary or leader of a mission)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch apostel, from Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos).

parole.significato: pharmacy, apothecary (a place where prescription drugs may be dispensed by an authorized pharmacologist)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch apoteke, from Latin apothēca. Doublet of boetiek and bodega.
From Late Latin archaicus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχαϊκός (arkhaïkós).
Borrowed from New Latin archaismus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχαϊσμός (arkhaïsmós).
Ultimately from Latin archaeologia, from Ancient Greek ἀρχαιολογία (arkhaiología).
From Latin archetypum (“original”), from Ancient Greek ἀρχέτυπον (arkhétupon, “model, pattern”).
Borrowed from Latin architectonicus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτεκτονικός (arkhitektonikós).
From Latin arōmaticus, from Ancient Greek ἀρωματικός (arōmatikós). By surface analysis, aroma + -isch.

parole.significato: arum, plant or flower of the genus Arum
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aron (also arum), from Ancient Greek ἄρον (áron).

From Latin arsenicum, from Ancient Greek ἀρσενικόν (arsenikón, “yellow arsenic”) (influenced by ἀρσενικός (arsenikós, “potent, virile”)), from Semitic (compare Classical Syriac ܙܪܢܝܟܐ (zarnīḵā), Aramaic 𐡆𐡓𐡍𐡉𐡊𐡀 (zrnykʾ /⁠zarnīḵā⁠/)), from Middle Iranian *zarnīk (compare Persian زرنی (zarni, “arsenic”
From Middle Dutch asbeston, from Latin asbestos, from Ancient Greek ἄσβεστος (ásbestos).

parole.significato: ascetic, one who lives a life of self-denial
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ascēta, from Ancient Greek ἀσκητής (askētḗs).
Borrowed from Latin ascēsis, from Ancient Greek ἄσκησις (áskēsis).
From Middle Dutch aspis, (ultimately) from Latin aspis, from Ancient Greek ἀσπίς (aspís).

parole.significato: aster, flowering plant of the genus Aster
parole.testo: From Latin astēr, from Ancient Greek ἀστήρ (astḗr). Named after the flower's semblance to a star.
Borrowed from Latin āsthma, from Ancient Greek ἆσθμα (âsthma).

From Middle Dutch astrologie, from Latin astrologia (“astronomy”), from Ancient Greek ἀστρολογία (astrología, “telling of the stars”), from ἄστρον (ástron, “star, planet, or constellation”) + -λογία (-logía, “treating of”), combination form of -λόγος (-lógos, “one who speaks (in a certain manner)”).

parole.significato: astronomy, the natural science branch studying the physical universe beyond Earth's atmosphere
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch astronomie, from Latin astronomia, from Ancient Greek ἀστρονομία (astronomía), ἄστρον (ástron, “star”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”). Equivalent to astro- + -nomie.

parole.significato: ataxia, pathological lack of coordination in bodily movements
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ataxia, from Ancient Greek ἀταξία (ataxía, “disorder”), derived from ἄτακτος (átaktos, “disorderly”).

parole.significato: a type of secondary education which is in curriculum identical to a gymnasium except that it does not offer classes in…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Athēnaeum, from Ancient Greek Ἀθηναῖον (Athēnaîon).

parole.significato: atlas (bound or digital collection of maps)
parole.testo: Apparently coined in Latin in this sense by Gerardus Mercator from the name of the mythological giant Atlas. Borrowed from Latin Atlas, from Ancient Greek Ἄτλας (Átlas).

parole.significato: athlete (a person who actively participates in physical sports, esp. one highly skilled in sports)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin āthlēta, from Ancient Greek ἀθλητής (athlētḗs).

parole.significato: the auditorium or main hall of a school or university
parole.testo: From Latin aula, from Ancient Greek αὐλή (aulḗ, “courtyard”).
Borrowed from Latin aura, from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra).
Borrowed from Latin autonomia, from Ancient Greek αὐτονομία (autonomía).
From New Latin autopsia, from Ancient Greek αὐτοψία (autopsía, “seeing with one's own eyes”).
Borrowed from Latin axiōma, from Ancient Greek ἀξίωμα (axíōma).

parole.significato: bacterium, any member of the domain Bacteria
parole.testo: Dutchification of older bacterium, from New Latin bactērium, from Ancient Greek βακτήριον (baktḗrion, “small staff”), from βακτηρία (baktēría).
Ultimately from Latin balaena (“whale”), from Ancient Greek φάλαινα (phálaina, “whale”). Cognate with English baleen.
From Middle Dutch balsame, from Latin balsamum, from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon). Doublet of bisam.
Borrowed from Latin basilica, from Ancient Greek βασιλική (basilikḗ).

parole.significato: basil, name of some plants of the mint family, notably:
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin basilicum (“royal robe”), substantive of basilicus (“royal, princely”), from Ancient Greek βασιλικός (basilikós, “royal”).

parole.significato: a basilisk (mythological or heraldic monster, part serpent, part rooster)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch basilisc, from Latin basiliscus, from Ancient Greek βασιλίσκος (basilískos).

parole.significato: beaker, cup, chalice (drinking vessel, often but not always without a handle, generally not made of glass)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch beker, from Latin bicarium, probably a diminutive of Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos, “amphora”). Cognate with English beaker.
Borrowed from New Latin bibliographia, from Ancient Greek βιβλιογραφία (bibliographía).

parole.significato: bishop (official in Orthodox, Catholic and some Protestant churches overseeing a diocese)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bischop, from Old Dutch biskop, from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos). The use of the term for mulled wine probably derived from English or German. The chess sense is likely a semantic loan from English bishop.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin blasphēmia, from Ancient Greek βλασφημία (blasphēmía, “profanity”), from βλασφημέω (blasphēméō, “to slander”).
Calque of Latin bona annūntiātiō, itself a calque from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion), or directly calqued from the Ancient Greek.
From bloem (“flower”) + lezing (“reading”), a calque of Latin florilegium, itself a calque of Ancient Greek ἀνθολογία (anthología), from ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”) + -λογία (-logía, “reading”).
Borrowed from Latin bōlētus, from Ancient Greek βωλίτης (bōlítēs). Cf. German Pilz.
Borrowed from Latin bōlus, from Ancient Greek βῶλος (bôlos).

parole.significato: a pair of glasses or goggles
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch beril (“beryl”), from Latin beryllus (“beryl”), from Ancient Greek βήρυλλος (bḗrullos), from Prakrit [Term?] (compare Sanskrit वैडूर्य (vaiḍūrya, “a cat's eye gem; a jewel”)), from Dravidian. Probably named after the city Velur (modern day Belur) in southern India. The first glasse
Borrowed from Latin būcolicus, from Ancient Greek βουκολικός (boukolikós).

parole.significato: cactus, plant of the family Cactaceae
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cactus, from Ancient Greek κάκτος (káktos, “cardoon”), of pre-Greek origin.

parole.significato: cannabis, plant of the genus Cannabis, especially Cannabis sativa or Cannabis indica
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cannabis, from Ancient Greek κάννᾰβῐς (kánnăbĭs). Doublet of hennep and canvas.
Borrowed from Late Latin catalogus, from Ancient Greek κατάλογος (katálogos, “enrollment, register, list, catalogue”).
From Middle Dutch cataracte, from Latin cataracta, from Ancient Greek καταρράκτης (katarrháktēs).
Borrowed from Latin catēchūmenus, from Ancient Greek κατηχούμενος (katēkhoúmenos).
Borrowed from Latin categoricus, from Ancient Greek [Term?]. Equivalent to categorie + -isch.
Ultimately from Latin centaurus, from Ancient Greek κένταυρος (kéntauros).
From Middle Dutch chaldeen (plural), from Latin Chaldaeus, from Ancient Greek Χᾰλδαῖος (Khăldaîos).
From Middle Dutch caos, from Latin chaos, from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos). Doublet of gas.

parole.significato: chemistry, the branch of natural science studying the composition and properties of matter
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin chimia, from Ancient Greek χυμεία (khumeía).
More recent than cherubijn. Borrowed from Latin cherūb, from Ancient Greek χερούβ (kheroúb), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew כְּרוּב (k'rúv).

From Middle Dutch cherubyn, cherubin, reanalyzed as singular, borrowed from Latin cherubin or cherubim, from Ancient Greek χερουβίμ (kheroubím), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew כְּרוּבִים (k'ruvím), which is originally plural.
Borrowed from Latin chylus, from Ancient Greek χυλός (khulós, “animal or plant juice”).
Borrowed from Latin cholera, from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra).

From Middle Dutch cristen, variant of kersten, from Old Dutch cristīn, from Latin Christiānus, from Ancient Greek Χρῑστιᾱνός (Khrīstiānós). The current Dutch spelling has been influenced by the Latin and subsequently also the Greek words.
Borrowed from New Latin chronicus, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós).
From Middle Dutch cythaer, from Old Dutch cithara, borrowed from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára, “kind of harp”).

parole.significato: climax (culmination of a narrative's rising action)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin climax, from Ancient Greek κλῖμαξ (klîmax).
Borrowed from New Latin clītoris, from Ancient Greek κλειτορίς (kleitorís).
Borrowed from Latin colophon, from Ancient Greek κολοφών (kolophṓn).
Borrowed from Latin coma, from Ancient Greek κῶμα (kôma).
Borrowed from Latin coma, from Ancient Greek κόμη (kómē).

parole.significato: a coreopsis, a plant in the genus Coreopsis of composite herbs
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin Coreopsis, from Ancient Greek κόρις (kóris, “bedbug”) + New Latin -opsis (“resembling structure”) (from Ancient Greek ὄψις (ópsis, “aspect, appearance”)).
Borrowed from Latin corōna, from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē). Doublet of kroon and kruin.
Borrowed from Latin crisis, from Ancient Greek κρίσις (krísis).

parole.significato: criterion, standard for comparison and appreciation
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin critērium, from Ancient Greek κριτήριον (kritḗrion).
Borrowed from Latin criticus, from Ancient Greek κρῐτῐκός (krĭtĭkós).

parole.significato: cyanogen, a blueish, acid, poisonous gas
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cȳaneus, from Ancient Greek κύανος (kúanos).
Borrowed from Latin cyclus, from Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”).
Borrowed from Latin cynicus, from Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós).

parole.significato: cyst (sac which develops in the natural cavities of an organ)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin cystis, from Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis).
Borrowed from Latin dactylus, from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos).
From Middle Dutch dadele. Ultimately from Latin dactylus, from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos), with the sense “date” probably deriving from a Semitic language.

parole.significato: any being that made the universe out of primal matter, demiurge
parole.testo: From New Latin dēmiūrgus (“demiurge”), from Ancient Greek δημιουργός (dēmiourgós, “craftsman”) after Platonic usage.
From Latin daemon (“lar, genius, guardian spirit”), from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn, “dispenser, god, protective spirit”).

From New Latin diabetes mellitus, from Ancient Greek διαβαίνω (diabaínō, “to pass through”), via the agent noun διαβήτης (diabḗtēs, “passing through”). This refers to the excessive amounts of urine produced by sufferers.

parole.significato: aperture (something which restricts the diameter of the light path through one plane in an optical system)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch diafragma, from Latin diaphragma, from Ancient Greek δῐᾰ́φρᾰγμᾰ (dĭắphrăgmă).

parole.significato: deacon (person involved in an ecclesiastical lay office for social affairs and charity)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch diaken, from Ecclesiastical Latin diāconus, from Ancient Greek διᾱ́κονος (diā́konos, “servant, minister”).
Borrowed from Latin dilemma, from Ancient Greek δίλημμα (dílēmma).
Borrowed from Latin diplōma, from Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma). The sense “diploma” derived from French diplôme.
Borrowed from Latin discus, from Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos). First attested in the eighteenth century.
From Latin diūrēticus, from Ancient Greek διουρητικός (diourētikós).

parole.significato: a Docete, an advocate of docetism, one of the Docetae
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Latin Docetae, ultimately from Ancient Greek δοκέω (dokéō, “to appear, to seem”).

parole.significato: dogma (colloquially with connotations of strictness and inflexibility)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dogma, from Ancient Greek δόγμα (dógma).

parole.significato: dogmatic (colloquially with connotations of strictness and inflexibility)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dogmaticus, from Ancient Greek δογμᾰτῐκός (dogmătĭkós). Equivalent to dogma + -isch.

parole.significato: dolphin, sea mammal of the family Delphinidae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch delfijn, from Latin delphīnus, from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís). Cognate with English dolphin.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσις (dósis, “a portion prescribed”, literally “a giving”), from Proto-Hellenic *dótis, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₃tis.

parole.significato: drama (theatrical work; anything involving play acting)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin drāma, from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma).
Borrowed from Latin dramaticus, from Ancient Greek δραματικός (dramatikós). Equivalent to drama + -icus.

parole.significato: stave, plank of the wall of a barrel
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch duge, from Latin doga, from Ancient Greek δοχή (dokhḗ).
From Middle Dutch echo, from Latin ēchō, from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ), from ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound”).
Ultimately from Latin eclecticus, from Ancient Greek ἐκλεκτικός (eklektikós).

parole.significato: an eczema, generic term for itchy and/or defiguring inflammations of the skin
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin eczema, constructed from Ancient Greek ἔκζεμα (ékzema, “rash”).

parole.significato: Aegean, referring to the mythological figure Aegaeus
parole.testo: From Latin Aegaeus, from Ancient Greek Αἰγαῖος (Aigaîos), + -isch.
Ultimately from Latin electrum (“amber; electrum”), from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron, “amber; electrum”).

parole.significato: electrum (naturally occurring alloy of gold and silver)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin electrum (“amber; alloy of gold and silver”), from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron).
Borrowed from Latin ellipsis, based on Ancient Greek ἔλλειψις (élleipsis, “omission”). Perhaps influenced by French ellipse.
Learned borrowing from Latin emblēma, from Ancient Greek ἔμβλημα (émblēma). Subsequently influenced by French emblème.
Learned borrowing from New Latin embryo, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon, “fetus”).
Borrowed from Latin empīricus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπειρικός (empeirikós). By surface analysis, empirie + -isch.

Borrowed from Latin emporium (“trading station, market town, market”); from Ancient Greek ἐμπόριον (empórion, “trading station”), from ἔμπορος (émporos, “merchant", "traveller", literally "incomer"”), from ἐν (en, “in”) and πόρος (póros, “journey”).
From New Latin empyema, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύημα (empúēma, “internal pustulence”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin endothēlium, from Ancient Greek ἔνδον (éndon, “endo-”) + θηλή (thēlḗ, “nipple”) + -ium (“aggregation”).
From Middle Dutch engel, from Old Dutch engil, from Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos).
Borrowed from Latin aenigma, from Ancient Greek αἴνιγμα (aínigma).

From Late Latin entelechia, from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia), coined by Aristotle from ἐντελής (entelḗs, “complete, finished, perfect”) (from τέλος (télos, “end, fruition, accomplishment”)) + ἔχω (ékhō, “to have”).
Borrowed from Latin aeon, from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn, “age”).
Borrowed from Latin epenthesis, from Ancient Greek ἐπένθεσις (epénthesis), from ἐπεντίθημι (epentíthēmi, “to insert”).
Learned borrowing from Latin Epicureus, from Ancient Greek Ἐπικούρειος (Epikoúreios).
Borrowed from Latin epicus but with a semantic shift inspired by other nouns on -icus, from Ancient Greek ἐπικός (epikós).
From Middle Dutch [Term?], from Latin epidemia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδήμιος (epidḗmios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + δῆμος (dêmos, “people”).
Borrowed from Latin epidermis, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδερμίς (epidermís).
Ultimately from Latin epiphania, from Ancient Greek ἐπιφάνεια (epipháneia).
From Middle Dutch epilencie, from Latin epilencia, variant of epilēpsia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιληψία (epilēpsía).
Learned borrowing from Latin epilēpticus, By surface analysis, epilepsie + -icus.
Borrowed from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos).

parole.significato: epistle; a literary composition in the form of a letter
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch epistele, from Latin epistola, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ), from ἐπιστέλλω (epistéllō, “to send a message”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to prepare, send”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin epithēlium, from Ancient Greek ἐπί (epí, “on, atop, epi-”) + θηλή (thēlḗ, “nipple”) + -ium (“aggregation”).

parole.significato: epic (extended narrative poem, usually in dactylic hexametre)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epos, from Ancient Greek ἔπος (épos).
Borrowed from New Latin erythēma, from Ancient Greek ἐρύθημα (erúthēma, “a redness or flush on the skin”), from ἐρυθρός (eruthrós, “red”).
From Esculaap, the Greco-Roman god of healing, from Middle Dutch esculapius, from Latin Aesculapius, from Ancient Greek Ἀσκληπιός (Asklēpiós).
From Middle Dutch ether, from Latin aethēr, from Ancient Greek αἰθήρ (aithḗr).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ēthica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ēthicus, from Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós).
Ultimately from Latin euphonia, from Ancient Greek εὐφωνία (euphōnía).
Borrowed from Latin eunūchus, from Ancient Greek εὐνοῦχος (eunoûkhos).
From Middle Dutch ewangelie, from Latin evangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news, message”).
Borrowed from Latin phalanx, from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx), see English phalanx.
Borrowed from Latin pharmaceuticus, from Ancient Greek φαρμακευτικός (pharmakeutikós).
Ultimately from Latin phiala, from Ancient Greek φιάλη (phiálē). Related to fiool.
From Middle Dutch philosophie, from Latin philosophia, from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía).
From Middle Dutch fiole, ultimately from Latin phiala, from Ancient Greek φιάλη (phiálē). Related to fiaal.

parole.significato: firmament (vault or sphere of the heavens, seen as solid in older cosmologies; sky)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch firmament, from Latin firmāmentum, coined by Jerome in the Vulgate to render Ancient Greek στερέωμα (steréōma, “firm or solid structure”), which in turn translates Hebrew רקיע (“vault of heaven”).
From Latin phlegmone, inflammation beneath the skin, from Ancient Greek.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”).

parole.significato: physicist, scientist or amateur student of physics
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin physicus, ultimately from Ancient Greek φυσικός (phusikós).
Ultimately from Late Latin physiognomia, from Ancient Greek φυσιογνωμίᾱ (phusiognōmíā, “physiology”).
From Middle Dutch gagaet, from Latin gagātēs, from Ancient Greek γαγᾱ́της (gagā́tēs), possibly from Γάγας (Gágas, “a town and river in Lycia”). Doublet of git.

parole.significato: a Galatian (member of the Celtic population in Anatolia)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch galate, from Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek Γαλάτης (Galátēs).

parole.significato: a germander; any plant of genus Teucrium
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gamander, gamandrea, from Medieval Latin gamandrea, earlier chamaedrys, from Ancient Greek χαμαίδρῡς (khamaídrūs).
Borrowed from Latin gangraena, from Ancient Greek γάγγραινα (gángraina).

Compound of geit (“goat”) + -en- + melken (“to milk”) + -er, a calque of Latin caprimulgus meaning the same, which in turn represents a partial calque of Ancient Greek αἰγοθήλας (aigothḗlas). So named due to the ancient belief that nightjars stole milk from goats, a claim made in Historia animalium

parole.significato: a geranium, plant of the genus Geranium
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin geranium, from Ancient Greek γέρανος (géranos, “crane”); more at ooievaarsbek.

parole.significato: a gyre, circular motion, notably in astronomy
parole.testo: From Latin gyrus, from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros).
Ultimately from Latin gypsum, from Ancient Greek γύψος (gúpsos), probably from a Semitic language.

parole.significato: glossary, list of words with their definitions and/or other annotations
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin glossārium, from glossa (“obsolete or foreign word that requires explanation”), from Ancient Greek γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin glōttis, from Ancient Greek γλωττῐ́ς (glōttĭ́s).

From Late Latin gonorrhoea (perhaps via German Gonorrhoe, Gonorrhö), from Ancient Greek γονόῥροια (gonórhroia), from γόνος (gónos, “sperm”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “flow”), due the mucus having been mistaken for semen.

parole.significato: gorgon (female monster with snakes on her head)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gorgone, from Latin Gorgon, from Ancient Greek Γοργώ (Gorgṓ).

parole.significato: grammar (rules for speaking and writing a language)
parole.testo: From Latin grammatica, from Ancient Greek γραμματική (grammatikḗ, “skilled in writing”), from γράμμα (grámma, “line of writing”), from γράφω (gráphō, “write”), from Proto-Indo-European *gerebh- (“to scratch”).
Borrowed from Latin grammaticus, from Ancient Greek γραμματικός (grammatikós).

parole.significato: a type of secondary school (for 12- to 18-year-olds) which prepares students for university or vocational school, and w…
parole.testo: From Latin gymnasium, from Ancient Greek γυμνάσιον (gumnásion, “exercise, school”).
From Latin halos, from Ancient Greek ἅλως (hálōs, “disk of the sun or moon, ring of light around the sun or moon; threshing floor; disk of a shield”), itself of unknown origin.
From Middle Dutch Hebreeusc, ultimately from Latin hebraeus, from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos).

parole.significato: Hebrew (speaker of Hebrew; Israeli, Jew or Israelite)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hebraeus, from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos).

parole.significato: hecatomb, public sacrifice involving many sacrificial animals
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hecatombe, from Ancient Greek ἑκατόμβη (hekatómbē).
Borrowed from Latin helix, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix).
From Middle Dutch heremite, heremijt and eremijt, a borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin erēmīta, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs).

parole.significato: Hesychasm (Eastern Orthodox mystical movement in late-mediaeval Byzantium)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Medieval Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek [Term?].

parole.significato: a Hesychast (Eastern Orthodox mystic in late-mediaeval Byzantium)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Medieval Latin hesychasta, from Ancient Greek ἡσυχαστής (hēsukhastḗs), from ἡσυχάζειν (hēsukházein, “to be quiet”), from ἥσυχος (hḗsukhos, “quiet”).

parole.significato: a hip prosthesis, artificial replacement for a hip
parole.testo: From heup (“hip”) + prothese (“prosthesis”) (from Late Latin prothesis, from Ancient Greek).
Borrowed from Latin hexameter, from Ancient Greek ἑξάμετρος (hexámetros).
From Middle Dutch historie, from Latin historia, from Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía).

From Middle Dutch holocaust, from Latin holocaustum, from the neuter of Ancient Greek ὁλόκαυστος (holókaustos). The shift to masculine was influenced by Middle French holocauste. The meaning “genocide” derives from English holocaust.
From Middle Dutch hontdage, a calque of Latin diēs caniculārēs (“puppy days”), itself a calque of Ancient Greek κυνάδες ἡμέραι (kunádes hēmérai, “dog days”). Equivalent to hond + -s- + dagen.
Borrowed from Latin horizōn, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).
Borrowed from Latin hyacinthus, from Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (huákinthos).

parole.significato: hyena, any member of the family Hyaenidae
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hyaena, from Ancient Greek ὕαινα (húaina).
From Latin hyperbolē, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολή (huperbolḗ, “excess, exaggeration”), from ὑπέρ (hupér, “above”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”).

parole.significato: the fake quality hypocrisy (claim, pretense, or false representation of holding beliefs, feelings, or virtues that one…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ypokrosie, itself directly from Latin hypocrisis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόκρισις (hupókrisis, “acting on the stage, pretense”).
From Latin hypothēca (“pledge, mortgage”), from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē, “warning, pledge”).
From Middle Dutch ibis, from Latin ibis, from Ancient Greek ἶβις (îbis), from Egyptian hbj.

parole.significato: an icon (religious image of a saint)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īcōn, from Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn, “likeness, image, portrait”). Eastern Orthodox Church sense is attested from 1833. Computing sense first recorded in 1982.

parole.significato: ink (coloured fluid used for writing, painting etc.)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch inct (“ink”), from Latin encaustum (“the red ink used by Roman and Greek rulers to sign documents”), from Latin encaustus (“paint technique using wax burning”), from Ancient Greek ἔγκαυστον (énkauston, “burned-in”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + καίω (kaíō, “burn”). Related to Dutch encaust

parole.significato: insect, arthropod of the class Insecta
parole.testo: Originally having a wider meaning (sense 2), as in Aristotle. From Latin īnsectum (“bug; cut up”), from īnsecō (“to cut up into”). The Latin is a calque of Ancient Greek ἔντομον (éntomon, “bug”), from ἔντομος (éntomos).
From Latin io, from Ancient Greek ἰώ (iṓ). Doublet of jo.
From New Latin ischaemia, from Ancient Greek ἴσχαιμος (ískhaimos, “stoppage of blood flow”).
Borrowed from Latin ischias, from Ancient Greek ἰσχιάς (iskhiás).

parole.significato: an Israelite, a member of ancient Israel
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch israelite, from Latin Isrāēlīta, from Ancient Greek Ἰσραηλίτης (Israēlítēs).
Borrowed from Latin īthyphallicus, from Ancient Greek ἰθυφαλλικός (ithuphallikós).

From Middle Dutch jōde, from Old Dutch judo, from Latin iūdaeus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos). The soccer sense ("supporter of AFC Ajax") refers to the fact that the club Ajax hails from Amsterdam, a city with a traditionally large Jewish community. While supporters from rivaling clubs oft
Learned borrowing from Latin calamus, from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos). Doublet of halm.

parole.significato: camel (Bactrian camel (Camelus bactrianus); animal of the genus Camelus)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch camêel, from Latin camēlus, from Ancient Greek κάμηλος (kámēlos), from a Semitic language. The form kemel (with stress on the initial syllable), the earliest attested form of the word in Middle Dutch which survived into early Modern Dutch, presumably represents an earlier borrowing

parole.significato: a room, physical chamber in a building
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch cāmere (“room, barn, house”), from Old Dutch *kamara, from Latin camera (“room, vault”), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “vaulted chamber”).

From Middle Dutch camille, from older camomille, from Latin camomilla, from Ancient Greek χαμαίμηλον (khamaímēlon). The shortened form (ca. 1460) was probably influenced by German Kamille (before 1350).

parole.significato: a canon, a cleric subject to an ecclesiastical rule
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch canonec, from Ecclesiastical Latin canonicus, from Ancient Greek κανονικός (kanonikós).
Borrowed from Latin catheter, from Ancient Greek καθετήρ (kathetḗr).
Borrowed from Latin catholicus, from Ancient Greek κᾰθολῐκός (kătholĭkós).
From Middle Dutch kelc, from Old Dutch kelik, from Latin calix, calyx, from Ancient Greek κᾰ́λῠξ (kắlŭx).

parole.significato: Celt, person of Celtic origin, (historical) member of a Celtic tribe
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Celtae (singular Celta), from Ancient Greek Κελτοί (Keltoí) (singular Κελτός (Keltós)). The singular is first attested in the sixteenth century, but remains rare until the nineteenth century.

parole.significato: a cherry tree, one of certain trees of the genus Prunus, especially the subgenus Cerasus
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch kerse, ultimately from Vulgar Latin ceresia, from the neuter plural of Late Latin ceresium, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”), ultimately possibly of Anatolian origin.
From Latin caerefolium, chaerephyllum, from Ancient Greek χαιρέφυλλον (khairéphullon).
From Middle Dutch ketter, from Latin catharus (“Cathar”), from Ancient Greek καθαροί (katharoí, “the pure”), originally used by practitioners of Novatianism in relation to themselves.

From Late Latin clēricus (“a priest, clergyman, cleric, also generally a learned man, clerk”), from Ancient Greek κληρικός (klērikós, “(adj. in church jargon) of the clergy”), from κλῆρος (klêros, “lot, inheritance,” originally “a shard used in casting lots”).
From Latin cōmoedia, from Ancient Greek κωμῳδία (kōmōidía).

From Middle Dutch comijn. Ultimately from Latin cumīnum, from Ancient Greek κύμινον (kúminon). The word had already entered early West Germanic as *kumīn (also *kumil), but such a form should have umlaut and initial stress in Dutch (*keumen). Therefore borrowed anew from Old French comin, or at leas

parole.significato: straight line connecting two dots of a curve
parole.testo: From Latin chorda, from Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ, “string of gut, the string of a lyre”). Doublet of koord.
Borrowed from Latin crātēr, from Ancient Greek κρᾱτήρ (krātḗr).
From Middle Dutch crocodil, from Latin crocodīlus, from Ancient Greek κροκόδειλος (krokódeilos).
Learned borrowing from Latin crocus, from Ancient Greek κρόκος (krókos), from a Semitic language.
From Middle Dutch cronike, borrowed from Latin chronica, from Ancient Greek χρονικόν (khronikón), neuter of χρονικός (khronikós).
From Latin cubus, from Ancient Greek κύβος (kúbos).

From Latin labyrinthus, from Ancient Greek λαβύρινθος (labúrinthos, “maze”), possibly from an Anatolian language (compare Lydian lábrus 'double-edged axe' and -inthos, a suffix typical of Anatolian placenames ), although the actual etymology of labyrinth is still a matter of conjecture.
From Middle Dutch lêec, leic, from Latin lāicus (“layman, laic”), from Ancient Greek λαϊκός (laïkós, “of the people”), from λαός (laós, “the people”).

Local dialect in the Dutch region Betuwe, from Latin lapathum (“kind of sorrel”), from Ancient Greek λάπαθον (lápathon, “kind of sorrel”). Probably via a form similar to ~*ledik, compare Old High German letihha.

parole.significato: lemma (proved or accepted proposition used in a proof)
parole.testo: From Latin lemma, from Ancient Greek λῆμμα (lêmma, “premise, assumption”), from λαμβάνω (lambánō, “to take”).
From New Latin lexicon, from Ancient Greek λεξικόν (lexikón, “a lexicon”), neuter of λεξικός (lexikós, “of words”).
From Middle Dutch liere, from Latin lyra, from Ancient Greek λύρα (lúra).

parole.significato: electuary (medicine mixed with honey or some kind of syrup)
parole.testo: Compound of likken (“to lick”) + -e- + pot (“pot, jar, vessel”), calque of Latin ēlectuārium, from Ancient Greek ἐκλεικτόν (ekleiktón). The sense “index finger” is likely influenced by a nursery rhyme collected by Johannes van Vloten.

parole.significato: litany (liturgical prayer consisting of series of prayers)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch letanie, from Latin letanīa, older litanīa, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía). The classical Latin and Greek forms with li- influenced the current Dutch spelling.

parole.significato: a liturgy, predetermined or prescribed set of (religious) rituals and associated customs, attributes etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin līturgia, from Ancient Greek λειτουργία (leitourgía, “work in public”).

From Latin logica, from Ancient Greek λογική (logikḗ, “logic”), from the feminine form of λογικός (logikós, “of or pertaining to speech or reason or reasoning, rational, reasonable”), from λόγος (lógos, “speech, reason”).

parole.significato: lotus, plant of the genus Nelumbo
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lōtus, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).
Borrowed from Latin Lyceum, from Ancient Greek Λύκειον (Lúkeion).

parole.significato: lynx (felid of the genus Lynx), also used of certain other medium-sized felids with large, plumed ears
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch linx, from Latin lynx, from Ancient Greek λύγξ (lúnx). Has largely displaced its inherited Germanic doublet los (“lynx”).
From Medieval Latin macrocosmus, formed from Ancient Greek μακρός (makrós, “long, great, grand”) + κόσμος (kósmos, “universe, order”).
Borrowed from Latin magma, from Ancient Greek μάγμα (mágma, “paste”).
From Middle Dutch magneet, from older magnes, from Latin magnēs, from Ancient Greek μαγνήτης λίθος (magnḗtēs líthos).
From Middle Dutch marmer, from Latin marmor, from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros).
Borrowed from Latin martyrium, from Ancient Greek μαρτύριον (martúrion).

parole.significato: martyrology (list of martyrs; hagiography about a martyr)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch martirologie, ultimately from Latin martyrologium, from Ancient Greek μαρτυρολόγιον (marturológion), but note that the word was already feminine in Middle Dutch.
Borrowed from Latin mathēmatica (“mathematics”), from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós, “mathematical”).

parole.significato: a mathematician, person studying or versed in mathematics
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mathēmaticus (“mathematician”), from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós, “fond of learning”), from μάθημα (máthēma, “knowledge, learning”).

Borrowed from Latin mausōlēum, from Ancient Greek Μαυσωλεῖον (Mausōleîon) from Ancient Greek Μαύσωλος (Maúsōlos); named for Mausolus (Μαύσωλος or Μαύσσωλλος), satrap of the Persian empire and ruler of Caria.
Borrowed from Latin maeander, Maeander, from Ancient Greek Μαίανδρος (Maíandros).
From Latin mechanismus, from Ancient Greek μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “machine”).
Borrowed from Latin melissa, from Ancient Greek μέλισσα (mélissa).
From Latin Messīās.

From Latin meteorum, from Ancient Greek μετέωρον (metéōron), from μετέωρος (metéōros, “raised from the ground, hanging, lofty”), from μετά (metá, “in the midst of, among, between”) (English meta) + ἀείρω (aeírō, “to lift, to heave, to raise up”). Original sense of “atmospheric phenomenon” gave rise

parole.significato: a metaphor by which an inclusive term stands for something included, or vice versa; a metaphor in which a part is spoke…
parole.testo: From Late Latin metonymia, from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).
From Latin mētropolis, from Ancient Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis, “mother city”).
Borrowed from Latin metrum, from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron). Doublet of meter.
First attested in 1778. Borrowed from New Latin miasma, from Ancient Greek μίασμα (míasma, “stain, pollution”).
From New Latin micro- (“small”), from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”).

From Mie, a contraction of the common Dutch name Marie, from Maria, from Vulgate Latin Maria, from Ancient Greek Μαρία (María), Μαριάμ (Mariám), from Aramaic מרים (Maryām), corresponding to the Hebrew מרים (Miryām).
Inherited from Middle Dutch minotaurus, from Latin minōtaurus, from Ancient Greek Μινώταυρος (Minṓtauros). Equivalent to common-noun use of Minotaurus.
From Middle Dutch moabite, from Latin mōabitēs, from Ancient Greek [Term?]. Equivalent to Moab + -iet.
From Middle Dutch monarcha, from Latin monarcha, from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs), variant of μόναρχος (mónarkhos, “sole ruler”), from 'μόνος (mónos, “only”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “leader”).
Ultimately from Latin monasticus, from Ancient Greek μοναστιχός (monastikhós).
From Middle Dutch monopolie, from Latin monopōlium, from Ancient Greek μονοπώλῐον (monopṓlĭon).
From Middle Dutch monster, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Latin monastērium (“monastery”), from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion).

parole.significato: musician (a person who plays or sings music)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mūsicus, from Ancient Greek μουσικός (mousikós).
Borrowed from Latin Mūsa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).
From Latin mysterium, ultimately from Ancient Greek μυστήριον (mustḗrion).
Borrowed from Latin mythos m, from Ancient Greek μῦθος m (mûthos).

From Latin nanus (“dwarf”), from Ancient Greek νᾶνος (nânos).
Borrowed from Latin narcissus, from Ancient Greek νάρκισσος (nárkissos).
First attested in the 20th century. Probably a borrowing, compare English narcist and German Narzisst. Ultimately from Latin Narcissus, from Ancient Greek Νάρκισσος (Nárkissos).
Borrowed from Latin necromantīa, from Ancient Greek νεκρομαντεία (nekromanteía). By surface analysis, necro- + -mantie.

parole.significato: necrosis, localized death of cells or living tissue
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin necrōsis, from Ancient Greek νέκρωσις (nékrōsis).
From Nijl (“Nile”) + paard (“horse”), a loose calque of Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos). The same in German Nilpferd.

parole.significato: nymph, female lesser divinity of nature
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch nymphe. Borrowed from Old or Middle French, from Latin nympha, borrowed from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē), of uncertain origin.
From Middle Dutch oester, from Latin ostrea, from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon).
From Middle Dutch ōlie, from Old Dutch olig, from Latin oleum, from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion).

parole.significato: onager, Asiatic wild ass, Equus hemionus
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin onager, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὄναγρος (ónagros, “wild ass”), from ὄνος (ónos, “ass, donkey”) + ᾰ̓́γρῐος (ắgrĭos, “wild”).
From Middle Dutch opium, from Latin opium, from Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion), from ὀπός (opós).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin orchis, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis).
From Middle Dutch organe, from Latin organum, from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon).
From Middle Dutch orgele, from earlier orgene, from Latin organa, plural of organum, from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon).

parole.significato: Slur for a Roman Catholic cleric.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pape (“priest, secular cleric”), from Old Dutch *papo (“priest”), from Latin papa, from Ancient Greek παπᾶς (papâs). Cognate to German Pfaffe. Doublet of paus.
Borrowed from Latin palladium, from Ancient Greek παλλάδιον (palládion, “statue of Pallas Athena”).
Ultimately from Late Latin pandemus, from Ancient Greek πάν (pán, “all”) + δῆμος (dêmos, “the people”).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin papȳrus, from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros).
Ultimately from Latin parabolicus, from Ancient Greek παραβολικός (parabolikós). Equivalent to parabool or parabel + -isch.

Borrowed from Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ), from παραβάλλω (parabállō, “to set side by side”), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”). Doublet of parool, parabel, and palaver.

parole.significato: paradigm (canonical or exhaustive set of inflected forms; set of forms with a common element)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma).

parole.significato: a paradise, wonderland, place to be
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch paradijs.

From Latin parallēlepipedum, from Ancient Greek παραλληλεπίπεδος (parallēlepípedos). While the spelling parallelepipedum does more justice to the etymology (as the word is essentially a compound of parallel and *epipedum) and is occasionally encountered, the unetymological reinterpretation parallell

parole.significato: anyone accompanying a bride or groom at their wedding, sometimes also taking the responsibility for its organisation
parole.testo: From Latin paranymphus, from Ancient Greek παράνυμφος (paránumphos, “friend of the bridegroom”).

From Middle Dutch prochie, from Latin parochia, from Ancient Greek πᾰροικῐ́ᾱ (păroikĭ́ā). The a was usually syncopated in Middle Dutch, but it was restored and became increasingly common in early modern Dutch due to influence of the Latin term.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin pasta (“dough, paste”), from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá, “barley porridge”). Displaced paste.
From Middle Dutch patriarch, from Latin patriarcha, from Ancient Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs).
Ultimately from Latin pericarpium, from Ancient Greek περικάρπιον (perikárpion).
Borrowed from Latin peritonaeum, from Ancient Greek περιτόναιον (peritónaion).
Ultimately from Latin petalum, from Ancient Greek πέτᾰλον (pétălon).
Borrowed from Latin petalum, from Ancient Greek πέτᾰλον (pétălon).
From Middle Dutch petercelie, petercelle, petersille, from Latin petroselinum, of Ancient Greek origin.
* From Latin petra (“stone, rock”), from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “stone, rock”).

parole.significato: petrochemistry, the branch of chemistry working mainly with components of fossile oil
parole.testo: the first syllable of petroleum (“Latin”) + chemie 'chemistry' (via Latin chimia ultimately from Ancient Greek)
Borrowed from Latin plasma, from Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma). Influenced by German Plasma (“blood plasma, cytoplasm”) and English plasma (“ionised gas”).

parole.significato: plectrum, pick (object for plucking certain string instruments)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin plēctrum, from Ancient Greek πλῆκτρον (plêktron).

From plaaster (“a plaster”), (perhaps via Old French plastre, modern plâtre) from Latin emplastrum, from Ancient Greek ἔμπλαστρον (émplastron, “salve, plaster”), from ἐν- (en-, “on”) + πλάσσω (plássō, “to mold, form”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin pleura, from Ancient Greek πλευρᾱ́ (pleurā́).
Borrowed from Latin podium, from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion, “base”), a diminutive of πούς (poús, “foot”). Doublet of pui.
Learned borrowing from Latin polīticus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós); corresponding to politiek + -icus. First attested in 1629.
From Latin polygamia, from Ancient Greek πολυγαμία (polugamía).

parole.significato: magnetic pole (especially of the Earth and other celestial bodies)
parole.testo: From Latin polus, which itself is from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos, “axis”). Cognate with English pole.
From Middle Dutch poëte, from Latin poēta, from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs). Doublet of pioet.
From Middle Dutch priester, from Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros). Cognate to English priest and German Priester.
Borrowed from Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma). First attested in the 17th century.
From Latin programma, from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma). Its usage in the sense of "computer program" is a semantic loan from English program.

parole.significato: propylon, monumental gate with pillars leading to the courtyard of a Greek or other ancient temple or palace
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin propylon, from Ancient Greek πρόπῠλον (própŭlon).

parole.significato: protasis, dependent clause of a conditional sentence
parole.testo: Ultimately derived from Late Latin protasis, from Ancient Greek πρότασις (prótasis).

parole.significato: the act of artificially replacing a body part
parole.testo: From Late Latin prothesis, from Ancient Greek; cognate with German Prothese, English prothese and (now more common) prosthesis and French prothèse.
Borrowed from New Latin Protista, from Ancient Greek πρώτιστος (prṓtistos).

From Middle Dutch psalter m. Likely not directly inherited from Old Dutch psaltare n, psaltere in this form, as the expected form (in accordance with Middle Dutch L-vocalization) is souter, an obsolete form which does appear to be inherited; see there for more. From Latin psychē, from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ).

parole.significato: purple, especially a reddish hue of purple (colour)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch purper, from Latin purpura, from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra).

parole.significato: a pygmy (member of an African tribe of short people)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pigmene (“Pygmies”), from Latin Pygmaeī, from Ancient Greek πυγμαῖος (pugmaîos).
From Latin pyro-, from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).

parole.significato: python, constrictor of the family Pythonidae
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Pythōn, from Ancient Greek Πύθων (Púthōn).
Borrowed from Latin pyxis, from Ancient Greek πυξίς (puxís). Doublet of box, buks (“shotgun”), and bus (“container”).
Borrowed from Latin rhīnocerōs, from Ancient Greek ῥῑνόκερως (rhīnókerōs).
From Latin rhētorica, from Ancient Greek ῥητορική (rhētorikḗ), feminine form of ῥητορικός (rhētorikós, “concerning public speech”), from ῥήτωρ (rhḗtōr, “public speaker”). retor + -ica.
From Latin rhētorica, from Ancient Greek ῥητορική (rhētorikḗ), feminine form of ῥητορικός (rhētorikós, “concerning public speech”), from ῥήτωρ (rhḗtōr, “public speaker”). retor + -iek.

First attested 1601, from Latin rheumatismus (“rheum”), from Ancient Greek ῥευματισμός (rheumatismós, “humour, discharge, rheum”) from ῥευματίζομαι (rheumatízomai, “to suffer from a rheum”) from ῥεῦμα (rheûma, “stream, flow”) from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”)
Borrowed from Latin rhonchus, from Ancient Greek ῥόγχος (rhónkhos).
Borrowed from Latin rhythmus, from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός (rhuthmós).
Borrowed from Latin rhododendron (“rosebay”), from Ancient Greek ῥοδόδενδρον (rhodódendron), from ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”) + δένδρον (déndron, “tree”).

parole.significato: a plant of the genus Ruta; rue
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch rute, from Latin rūta, from Ancient Greek ῥυτή (rhutḗ).
Borrowed from Latin sabbatum (“Sabbath”), from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (šabbāṯ).

parole.significato: sapphire (transparent blue corundum, or a clear corundum of another colour)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch saffier, from Latin sapphirus, from Ancient Greek σάπφειρος (sáppheiros).

parole.significato: salamander, amphibian of the order Caudata
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch salamander, from Latin salamandra, from Ancient Greek σαλαμάνδρα (salamándra).

parole.significato: salp, any member of the class Thaliacea
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin salpa (“stockfish”), from Ancient Greek σάλπη (sálpē, “a species of fish”).
From Middle Dutch sarasijn, from Latin Saracēnus, from Ancient Greek Σαρακηνός (Sarakēnós).
Ultimately from Latin satyrus, from Ancient Greek σάτυρος (sáturos).
Borrowed from Latin scepticus, from Ancient Greek σκεπτικός (skeptikós).

From Middle Dutch schandele, from Latin scandalum, from Ancient Greek σκᾰ́νδᾰλον (skắndălon). In early Modern Dutch the word was influenced by Middle French scandale, leading to stress on the final syllable with a full vowel.

parole.significato: a school, educational institution that provides education, whether combined with research or not
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch schôle, from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ). Doublet of skorro and sjoel.
Borrowed from New Latin selēnium, a word coined by Swedish chemist Berzelius in 1818, from Ancient Greek Σελήνη (Selḗnē, “moon”).
From Sem, Shem + -iet, from Late Latin Sēm, from Ancient Greek Σήμ (Sḗm), from Biblical Hebrew שם (šēm). Compare German Semit, New Latin Sēmīta, French sémite.

parole.significato: lilac, woody plant of the genus Syringa
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin syringa, from sȳrinx, from Ancient Greek σῦρῐγξ (sûrĭnx).

Borrowed from Latin sēsamum, from Ancient Greek σήσαμον (sḗsamon), from Old Aramaic שושמא (šūššmā), shortening of שומשומא (šumššemā), from Akkadian 𒃻𒈦𒌑𒈬 (/⁠šamaššammū⁠/), 𒊭𒈦𒌑𒈨 (/⁠šamaššammi⁠/, literally “oil plant”).
From Middle Dutch smaragd, from Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos), μάραγδος (máragdos), from a Semitic language.
Borrowed from Latin smēgma, from Ancient Greek σμῆγμα (smêgma).

parole.significato: a sodomite, a man who penetrates another man anally or (more generally) any male homosexual
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sodomite (“Sodomite, inhabitant of Sodom”), from Latin sodomīta, from Ancient Greek σοδομίτης (sodomítēs). Equivalent to Sodom + -iet.

parole.significato: sophism, the practices and doctrines of the sophists, ancient Greek itinerant teachers of rhetoric who taught a form of…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sophisme, from Latin sophisma, from Ancient Greek [Term?].
From Middle Dutch socke, from Latin soccus, from Ancient Greek σύκχος (súkkhos). The current sense derived from German Socke.
From Latin sorus, from Ancient Greek σωρός (sōrós).
From Latin spatula (“a flat piece”), which is a diminutive of the Latin spatha (“broad or flat tool”), itself coming from the Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “a broad wood or metal blade”).
From Late Latin sporangium, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá, “seed”) + ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “vessel”).

Borrowed from Latin stadium (“a measure of length, commonly one-eighth of a Roman mile, furlong; a race course”), from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion, “a measure of length, a running track”), especially the track at Olympia, which was one stadium in length. parole.significato: stigma (an indication of infamy or disgrace)
parole.testo: From Latin stigma, from Ancient Greek στίγμα (stígma, “mark of slavery or disgrace”).
Ultimately from Latin styrax, from Ancient Greek στύραξ (stúrax).

parole.significato: a person devoted to pleasure and luxury; a sybarite
parole.testo: From Latin Sybarita, from Ancient Greek Συβαρίτης (Subarítēs, “inhabitant of Subaris”), from Σύβαρις (Súbaris, “Sybaris, an ancient Greek city in southeastern Italy noted for the luxurious, pleasure-seeking habits of many of its inhabitants”).
From Latin synecdoche, from Ancient Greek συνεκδοχή (sunekdokhḗ, “receiving together”).
From Latin syntaxis, from Ancient Greek σῠ́ντᾰξῐς (sŭ́ntăxĭs).
Borrowed from Latin sȳrinx (“reed; reed pipe, panpipes”), from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “panpipes; pipe-shaped object”), from Pre-Greek.
Borrowed from Late Latin systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma, “organised whole, body”).
From Late Latin tautologia, from Ancient Greek ταὐτολογία (tautología) from ταὐτός (tautós, “the same”) + λόγος (lógos, “explanation”).
From Latin tectonicus, from Ancient Greek τεκτονικός (tektonikós). By surface analysis, tektoniek + -isch.

parole.significato: teleological, concerning or applying teleology, either in theological or physiological sense
parole.testo: From teleologie + -isch, itself from New Latin teleolog, coined 1728 by German philosopher Baron Christian von Wolff (1679-1754) from Ancient Greek τέλειος (téleios, “entire, perfect, complete”) + -λογία (-logía, “-logy”).

parole.significato: a tetrarch (governor or ruler of a quarter of a country)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin tetrarchēs, from Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “ruler, leader”).
From Latin thaumaturgus, from Ancient Greek θαυματουργός (thaumatourgós).
Borrowed from Latin thema, from Ancient Greek θέμα (théma).
Borrowed from Latin theōrēma, from Ancient Greek θεώρημα (theṓrēma).
Directly or ultimately from Latin thēsaurus, from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós).
From Middle Dutch tike, from Old Dutch *tīca, borrowed from Latin thēca, which is borrowed from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē).

parole.significato: tyrant, absolute ruler of an Ancient polis
parole.testo: From Latin tyrannus (“monarch, ruler; tyrant”), itself from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos, “tyrant”). The sense "tyrant flycatcher" corresponds to the taxonomic family name, taxonomic name Tyrannidae; more at tyrant flycatcher.
From Latin Titan, from Ancient Greek Τιτάν (Titán).

parole.significato: trapezium, trapezoid (four-sided shape with no sides parallel and no equal sides)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin trapezium, from Ancient Greek τρᾰπέζῐον (trăpézĭon, “irregular quadrilateral”), diminutive of τρᾰ́πεζα (trắpeza, “table”). First attested in 1654.

parole.significato: term used for typhus and typhoid fever
parole.testo: From New Latin typhus, from Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos, “fever, stupor”).

parole.significato: type: a class, someone or something from a class. The diminutive is used when made into a caricature
parole.testo: From Latin typus, from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark, impression, type”), from τύπτω (túptō, “to strike, beat”).
From type + -isch, after German typisch or French typique, borrowed from Late Latin typicus, derived from Ancient Greek τυπικός (tupikós).
Borrowed from Latin ūrēthra, from Ancient Greek οὐρήθρα (ourḗthra).

parole.significato: polygon (plane figure bounded by straight edges)
parole.testo: Compound of veel (“much, many”) + hoek (“angle, corner”), coined by Simon Stevin as a purism for Latin polygonum, therefore a calque of Ancient Greek πολύγωνον (polúgōnon).

parole.significato: a scalpel (sharp small knife with single 3-5 cm long cutting surface as used for surgery)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vlîme, vlieme, from older *vlît(e)me, *vliet(e)me, from Latin phlebotomus, from Ancient Greek φλεβότομος (phlebótomos). Cognate with Old High German fliodema (modern Fliete), Middle Low German vlêteme, Old English flītme, Old French flieme (English fleam).
From wijsheid (“wisdom”) + -s- + tand (“tooth”), calque of Latin dēns sapientiae, itself a calque of Ancient Greek σωφρονιστῆρες (sōphronistêres).
From Middle Dutch sēgene, seine, from Old Dutch *segina, from Latin sagēna, from Ancient Greek σαγήνη (sagḗnē).

parole.significato: zealot (anti-Roman Jewish insurrectionist in first-century Palestine, especially Judaea)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch zelote, from Latin zēlōtēs, from Ancient Greek ζηλωτής (zēlōtḗs).
From Middle Dutch zelote, from Latin zēlōtēs, from Ancient Greek ζηλωτής (zēlōtḗs).
From Middle Dutch sarc, serc, from Vulgar Latin *sarcus, from Latin sarcophagus, from Ancient Greek σαρκοφάγος (sarkophágos).
Borrowed from Latin zōna, from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē).

parole.significato: a zoologist, biologist specialised in the animal kingdom
parole.testo: From zoölogie (“zoology”) (cognate, from New Latin zoologia, constructed from Ancient Greek).
